items.prompt: In Scrum, who is accountable for maximizing the value of the product and for managing the Product Backlog?

options.label: The Developers
The Scrum Master
The project sponsor
The Product Owner

rubric: The Product Owner owns the Product Backlog and the product's value.
Distractors confuse this with the Scrum Master's coaching role or with outside sponsors.

items.prompt: What is the maximum length of a Sprint in Scrum?

options.label: One week
Six weeks
One month
Three months

rubric: Sprints are one month or less.
Longer options reflect a mix-up with traditional project phases.

items.prompt: What is the timebox of the Daily Scrum?

options.label: 30 minutes
60 minutes
5 minutes
15 minutes

rubric: The Daily Scrum is capped at 15 minutes.
Other values are common guesses for meetings in general.

items.prompt: Which artifact is the ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product, kept by the Product Owner?

options.label: Product Backlog
Sprint Backlog
Increment
Burndown chart

rubric: The Product Backlog is the ordered, evolving list of product work.
The Sprint Backlog covers only the current sprint.

items.prompt: Which Scrum event is held at the end of a Sprint so the team can plan improvements to how it works?

options.label: Sprint Planning
Daily Scrum
Sprint Retrospective
Sprint Review

rubric: The Retrospective focuses on improving the team's process.
The Sprint Review inspects the Increment, not the process.

items.prompt: Which of the following are official Scrum events? Select all that apply.

options.label: Sprint Planning
Change Control Board
Gantt Review
Sprint Review
Daily Scrum

rubric: Planning, Daily Scrum and Review are Scrum events.
Change Control Board and Gantt Review belong to traditional management, not Scrum.

items.prompt: At the start of a sprint, a team selects several items from the Product Backlog and writes a plan for delivering them. The team keeps this selection and plan visible all sprint. What is this artifact called?

options.label: Product Backlog
Increment
Sprint Backlog
Release roadmap

rubric: The Sprint Backlog holds the selected items plus the plan for the sprint.
The Product Backlog is the full list, not just the sprint's selection.

items.prompt: Why does Scrum use fixed-length Sprints?

options.label: They remove the need for separate planning and review meetings
They guarantee that every item planned for the Sprint is finished
They create a regular rhythm that brings frequent feedback
They let managers add new work to the Sprint at any moment

rubric: Fixed length creates a rhythm for inspection and adaptation.
Distractors assume sprints guarantee delivery or allow unlimited scope changes.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective?

options.label: The Review is held for managers only, the Retrospective for the Product Owner only
The Review plans the next sprint, the Retrospective estimates backlog items
The Review inspects the team's way of working, the Retrospective inspects the product
The Review inspects the Increment, the Retrospective inspects how the team works

rubric: Review is about the product Increment; Retrospective is about process.
The first distractor swaps the two purposes.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the Scrum Master's role?

options.label: A project manager who approves the plan before each sprint starts
A manager who assigns tasks to each Developer and tracks hours
A senior owner who decides the order of the Product Backlog
A servant-leader who helps the team understand and use Scrum

rubric: The Scrum Master coaches and removes impediments rather than commanding.
Distractors treat the role as traditional management or as the Product Owner's job.

items.prompt: Why does a Scrum team keep a shared Definition of Done?

options.label: It lists the tasks each Developer must do every day
It lets the Product Owner skip the Sprint Review if work looks done
It gives everyone the same understanding of when work is complete
It sets the exact number of hours allowed for each backlog item

rubric: The Definition of Done creates transparency about completeness.
Distractors confuse it with task lists, review waivers or time budgets.

items.prompt: A backlog item reads: "As a shopper, I want to save items to a wishlist so I can buy them later." How is this item best classified?

options.label: A sprint goal covering the whole sprint's outcome
A user story describing value from a user's view
A defect report describing a bug in released code
A retrospective action to improve team habits

rubric: The As a / I want / so that format is a user story.
Other options are different kinds of items with different purposes.

items.prompt: Which of the following reflect values stated in the Agile Manifesto? Select all that apply.

options.label: Responding to change over following a plan
Following a plan over responding to change
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools

rubric: The Manifesto favours responding to change, people, and working software.
Two options reverse the Manifesto's stated preferences.

items.prompt: Midway through a sprint, a stakeholder asks the team to add a new feature. The request does not threaten the current Sprint Goal. Which response is most consistent with Scrum?

options.label: The Scrum Master adds it to the Sprint Backlog and extends the sprint
The Product Owner adds it to the Product Backlog for ordering later
The Developers drop their current items and start the feature right away
The team ignores the request and never records it anywhere

rubric: New requests go to the Product Backlog and are ordered by the Product Owner.
Distractors break sprint stability or lose valuable feedback.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of the Sprint Review in Scrum?

options.label: To get managers to approve the sprint budget and sign off on the overall project schedule
To assess each developer's individual output and decide who needs coaching next sprint
To inspect the finished increment with stakeholders and gather feedback that shapes the backlog
To discuss how the team worked together and pick process changes for the next sprint

rubric: The review is about inspecting the product increment and adapting the backlog with stakeholders.
The last distractor describes the Retrospective, which is the common mix-up.

items.prompt: Which responsibility belongs to the Product Owner in a Scrum team?

options.label: Removing impediments and coaching the team on following Scrum rules
Ordering the product backlog so the most valuable work comes first
Assigning tasks to each developer and tracking their daily hours worked
Deciding the technical design the developers use to build each item

rubric: The Product Owner maximises product value by ordering the backlog.
Task assignment and technical design belong to developers; coaching and impediments belong to the Scrum Master.

items.prompt: What is a Definition of Done in Scrum?

options.label: A date agreed with stakeholders by which the whole product must be released
A list of features the product owner wants built over the next quarter
A shared checklist of what makes a backlog item complete enough to release
A statement of the sprint's goal written by the Scrum Master at planning

rubric: The Definition of Done is a shared quality standard for completed work.
Distractors confuse it with a release date, a roadmap or the sprint goal.

items.prompt: How is the Daily Scrum best described?

options.label: A session where the product owner reorders the backlog with stakeholders
A session at the end of each sprint to demo completed items to customers
A short timebox where developers sync on progress toward the sprint goal and adjust the plan
A status meeting where developers report hours spent and tasks finished to the project manager

rubric: The Daily Scrum is for developers to plan their work toward the sprint goal.
It is not a manager status report, a backlog session or a demo.

items.prompt: Which of these is a Scrum artifact rather than an event?

options.label: Sprint Retrospective
Product Backlog
Daily Scrum
Sprint Planning

rubric: Scrum artifacts are the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment.
The other options are events.

items.prompt: Which statements reflect values in the Agile Manifesto? Select all that apply.

options.label: Customer collaboration is valued over contract negotiation
Working software is valued over comprehensive documentation
Following a plan is valued over responding to change
Processes and tools are valued over individuals and interactions

rubric: The Manifesto favours working software and customer collaboration.
Two options reverse the Manifesto's preferences.

items.prompt: Halfway through a sprint, a stakeholder asks a developer to add a new feature right away. The team is on track for its sprint goal. According to Scrum, what is the most appropriate way to treat this request?

options.label: Pass it to the Product Owner, who can add it to the backlog and order it for a later sprint
Ask the Scrum Master to extend the sprint until the new feature is finished, so the sprint goal is still met
Refuse it and tell the stakeholder that Scrum never accepts changing requirements once a sprint has started
Add it to the sprint at once and have the developers drop whichever item they judge to be least important

rubric: The sprint goal stays stable; new requests go to the Product Owner for backlog ordering.
Distractors ignore the PO's role, extend the timebox or wrongly claim Scrum rejects change.

items.prompt: A team's velocity over the last three sprints was 20, 24 and 22 points. 110 points remain in the backlog. Using average velocity, about how many more sprints are needed?
rubric: Average velocity is 22, and 110 / 22 = 5 sprints.
Other values come from using the wrong velocity or rounding mistakes.

items.prompt: A Kanban board has a WIP limit of 3 on 'In Progress', and it already holds 3 cards. A developer has just finished their own card elsewhere. What should they do next?

options.label: Help finish or unblock a card already in progress before pulling anything new
Start a fourth card in the column since they have spare capacity right now
Split an existing card into two smaller cards so the column is no longer at its limit
Wait until the next planning meeting so the team can decide what to pull next

rubric: WIP limits mean finishing work in progress before pulling new work.
Starting a fourth card breaks the limit; splitting cards to dodge it defeats its purpose.

items.prompt: The story 'As a user, I can manage my account' is too big for one sprint. Which split best follows good Agile practice?

options.label: Smaller stories such as 'reset password' and 'update email', each usable alone
One story each for design, coding and testing of the whole feature, done in order
Separate stories for the database, the screens and the business logic, built by layer
Keep it whole and carry it across several sprints until it is finished

rubric: Stories should be split vertically into small slices that each deliver user value.
Splitting by layer or phase gives nothing usable until all parts finish.

items.prompt: In a retrospective, a team notes its Daily Scrum often runs 30 minutes because of long technical debates. Which action best applies Scrum practice?

options.label: Keep it to 15 minutes and take deep talks to a follow-up
Have the Scrum Master run it and decide who may speak and for how long each time
Invite stakeholders so the debates are settled in front of them, then record decisions
Cancel the Daily Scrum and replace it with a weekly written report from each member

rubric: The Daily Scrum is timeboxed to 15 minutes; detailed talks happen afterwards.
Other options remove the event, shift ownership or add the wrong audience.

items.prompt: Sprint capacity is 21 points. The ordered backlog is: A (13), B (8), C (5), D (3). Which items should the team pull into the sprint?

options.label: A, B and D
A and B
B, C and D
A, C and D

rubric: Items are pulled in priority order: A and B total exactly 21.
Skipping B for lower-priority items ignores the ordering, and A, B and D exceeds capacity.

items.prompt: Midway through a sprint, a team sees it cannot finish everything and the sprint goal is at risk. Which actions are consistent with Scrum? Select all that apply.

options.label: Extend the sprint by three days without telling anyone
Mark unfinished items as done so the sprint looks successful
Raise the risk at the Daily Scrum and re-plan the day's work
Have the developers and Product Owner renegotiate scope while protecting the sprint goal

rubric: Scrum handles risk by inspecting at the Daily Scrum and renegotiating scope with the PO.
Changing the timebox or faking completion breaks Scrum rules.

items.prompt: On the last day of a sprint, testing finds serious bugs in three backlog items, so they do not meet the Definition of Done. The team asks what to do with these items before the Sprint Review.

options.label: Carry them into the next sprint automatically, since the team has already started the work and the Product Owner should not reorder them
Treat them as not done, show only finished work, and return them to the backlog for reordering
Count them as done and log the bugs as new items, so that velocity reflects the work the team completed
Extend the sprint by two days so all three items can be finished and then shown at the Sprint Review

rubric: Items that miss the Definition of Done are not part of the increment and go back to the backlog for the PO to reorder.
Counting them as done, extending the sprint or auto-carrying them over all break Scrum rules.

items.prompt: A Scrum team's last three sprints delivered 28, 32 and 30 story points. The Product Backlog has 180 points of estimated work left and the team's capacity is stable. Using average velocity, how many sprints should the team forecast?

options.label: 5 sprints
7 sprints
8 sprints
6 sprints

rubric: Average velocity is 30, and 180 / 30 = 6 sprints.
Choosing 5 or 7 comes from using the best or worst sprint instead of the average.

items.prompt: For a 10-day sprint, a team of 5 has 50 person-days of raw time. One member is away for 2 days, and the team assumes an 80% focus factor for meetings and interruptions. What is the sprint capacity?

options.label: 48 person-days
50 person-days
40 person-days
38.4 person-days

rubric: Capacity = (50 - 2) x 0.8 = 38.4 person-days.
Distractors skip either the absence or the focus factor.

items.prompt: At the Daily Scrum, a developer says she cannot test her story because the staging environment has been down for two days. As Scrum Master, what is the best next step?

options.label: Take responsibility for getting staging restored through the right people and report back
Note it in the sprint report for the Product Owner and tell her to start another story
Ask her to hold it until the retrospective so the Daily Scrum stays on the Sprint Goal
Spend the whole Daily Scrum having the developers diagnose and repair staging together

rubric: Scrum Masters help remove impediments promptly, after the Daily Scrum rather than inside it.
Waiting for the retrospective or turning the event into a problem-solving session misreads the event's purpose.

items.prompt: Mid-sprint, the Product Owner asks to add an urgent 8-point item. The sprint is already full at 30 points, and the Sprint Goal is still achievable. According to Scrum, what should happen?

options.label: Refuse the item outright, because the sprint backlog is locked once sprint planning has ended
Add the item quietly and ask developers to work overtime to deliver all of the original and new work
Extend the sprint by two days so that both the original work and the urgent item fit in this sprint
Developers and the Product Owner negotiate, swapping out about 8 points of lower-priority work

rubric: Scope can be renegotiated mid-sprint with the Product Owner without endangering the Sprint Goal.
Extending the sprint or silently adding work breaks timeboxing and sustainable pace.

items.prompt: A story reads: 'As a shopper, I can pay for my order by card, PayPal or gift card.' It is too big for one sprint. Which split best follows good story-splitting practice?

options.label: Split by role into a coding story, a test-case story and a documentation story
Create separate database, API and UI tasks and deliver each in a different sprint
Deliver card payment end to end first, then add PayPal and gift card as separate stories
Keep one story and give each of three developers one payment method to build alone

rubric: Vertical slices deliver working, valuable functionality each sprint.
Layer-based or role-based splits produce nothing shippable until all parts are done.

items.prompt: A team's Definition of Done has three items only: code peer-reviewed, automated tests passing, and deployed to staging. At the sprint review, which stories can be counted as Done? Select all that apply.

options.label: Coded, reviewed, tests passing and deployed to staging
Reviewed, tests passing and deployed to staging, but the Product Owner has not yet looked at it
Coded and tests passing, with the review scheduled for next sprint
Coded, reviewed and on staging, but two automated tests are failing

rubric: A story is Done only when every item in the Definition of Done is met; Product Owner viewing is not listed.
Missing review or failing tests means the DoD is not met.

items.prompt: A team uses a Kanban board with a WIP limit of 4 on the 'In Review' column, and it currently holds 4 items. A developer finishes coding a ticket and is ready to move it forward. The backlog has plenty of ready tickets. What should the developer do?

options.label: Raise the review limit to 5 for now, since the finished ticket is already done coding and shouldn't sit idle
Leave the ticket in Coding and pick up a lower-priority bug fix, so the developer stays busy while review clears
Pull the next ticket from the backlog, since coding capacity is free and the review limit only applies to reviewers
Help review one of the four waiting items so the queue drains

rubric: WIP limits push the team to finish work before starting more, so swarming on review is right.
Raising the limit or starting new work hides the bottleneck.

items.prompt: A team's velocity alternates 40, 22, 41, 20. Its stories are mostly 8 or 13 points, and the largest ones are usually started in the last few days of a sprint. Which cause best explains the pattern?

options.label: Estimates are inflated in alternate sprints, because the team re-points stories after seeing a low velocity
Developers work harder in odd-numbered sprints, so effort rather than story size drives the swings in output
Big stories begun near sprint end spill over, so their points are counted in the next sprint
Velocity naturally oscillates in mature teams as they alternate between feature work and cleanup, so no investigation is needed

rubric: Unfinished large stories carry over and are counted in the following sprint, producing a sawtooth.
Other options blame motivation or treat the pattern as normal without evidence.

items.prompt: A team holds good retrospectives and writes actions on a wiki page, yet the same problems recur sprint after sprint. Which is the most likely underlying cause?

options.label: Actions have no owner and aren't in the sprint backlog, so they lose out to product work
The team picks too few actions each time, so the improvements stay too small for anyone to notice
The Scrum Master facilitates too strictly, so people avoid raising the real issues in the room
Retrospectives are too short, so the team never gets time to identify any of the real problems

rubric: Improvement actions need owners and a place in the sprint plan to compete for capacity.
The other options guess at facilitation or quantity without explaining recurrence of identified problems.

items.prompt: At sprint reviews, stakeholders nod but give little feedback. The team presents slides and mockups of work in progress. What is the underlying problem?

options.label: No working Increment is shown, so stakeholders can't react to real behaviour
Stakeholders are too senior, so only junior staff should be invited to the review
Reviews are too frequent, so there is rarely enough new content to discuss
Slides are too short, so adding technical architecture detail would prompt questions

rubric: The review is meant to inspect a working Increment; slides and mockups invite polite approval, not feedback.
Other options change audience or frequency without addressing what is being inspected.

items.prompt: A sprint burndown stays almost flat for eight of ten days, then drops steeply on the last two. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this?

options.label: The sprint is too long, so progress always looks flat until the final days
The team finished early and stopped updating the board once its goals were reached
Items are large and tested only at the end, so tasks close just before sprint end
Scope was added steadily, which alone explains a flat line followed by a cliff

rubric: Large items with late testing mean little is Done until the end, giving a flat-then-cliff line.
Sprint length alone and early finishing don't produce this specific shape.

items.prompt: In a team's Daily Scrum, each member reports hours worked to a manager, who then assigns tasks for the day. Which aspect most undermines how Scrum is meant to work?

options.label: Hours are reported, because Scrum prohibits any form of time tracking
Developers report what they did, which Scrum forbids; only plans may be shared
A manager assigns tasks, so developers don't self-organise around the Sprint Goal
It is held at the same time each day, which makes it stale and routine

rubric: The Daily Scrum is for developers to plan their own work toward the Sprint Goal; external task assignment removes self-management.
Fixed timing is deliberate, and Scrum doesn't forbid sharing progress or tracking hours.

items.prompt: A Product Owner role is meant to be empowered to order the backlog and accept work. Which observed behaviours suggest this Product Owner is not truly empowered? Select all that apply.

options.label: The backlog is reordered after each review based on stakeholder feedback
The Product Owner needs a director's sign-off before accepting any story as done
Every backlog ordering decision is sent to a steering committee for approval
Developers get answers to clarifying questions within a few hours during the sprint

rubric: Needing external approval for ordering and acceptance shows decision authority sits elsewhere.
Answering questions quickly and reordering after feedback are normal, healthy Product Owner behaviour.

items.prompt: A team commits to 35 points per sprint but completes about 20. Developers build all stories first, then hand them to QA in the last three days. QA finds defects, and the stories roll over. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Developers write poor code, so a stricter review gate before planning would fix it
QA staff are too slow, so adding more testers is the only change needed
Testing starts only after all development ends, so no time remains to fix defects
The 35-point commitment is too ambitious, so velocity should simply be forced down to 20

rubric: Handing everything to QA at the end is a mini-waterfall; defects surface when there is no time to fix them.
Lowering commitment, adding testers or gating reviews treat symptoms without changing the flow of work.

items.prompt: A team's velocity held at about 30 points for six sprints. Two new developers join, and the next sprint delivers only 22 points. Which analysis best explains the dip?

options.label: Existing members spend capacity on onboarding and knowledge transfer, so a short-term dip is expected and not proof of lower skill.
The new developers are working slower than the team estimated, so the team should raise the estimates on every backlog item before the next sprint.
Added headcount raises velocity at once, so the dip suggests the Scrum Master has not enforced the Definition of Done in the last sprint.
Velocity is meaningful only for teams with stable membership, so the team should drop it and commit to a fixed number of stories per sprint.

rubric: New members consume existing members' capacity at first, so a temporary dip is a normal team-change effect.
Distractors wrongly blame individuals, assume headcount scales linearly, or discard the metric.

items.prompt: In a 10-day sprint, the burndown chart stays almost flat for seven days and then drops steeply to zero by day 10. What does this pattern most likely indicate?

options.label: The Product Owner is adding scope each day, which keeps the line flat until the scope is finally frozen on day seven.
The Daily Scrum is too short, so impediments are not raised until the team finally decides to finish everything at once.
Stories are too large and are finished together near the end instead of being completed in small, steadily delivered slices.
The team is estimating too pessimistically, so most work is done early but only recorded on the final days of the sprint.

rubric: A flat-then-cliff burndown signals large items that are only 'done' at the end, hiding risk.
Other options invent causes not suggested by the pattern.

items.prompt: At the Daily Scrum, each developer reports what they did yesterday to the Scrum Master, who writes it down, and the meeting ends without discussing the Sprint Goal. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: The event is too short, and extending it to an hour would give the team room to plan the whole sprint again.
The event has become status reporting to a manager instead of developers coordinating their work toward the Sprint Goal.
The event is working properly, since each person gives an update and the Scrum Master gets full visibility of progress.
The event should be replaced by a written report, because verbal updates fail to capture the detail that stakeholders need.

rubric: The Daily Scrum is for developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and replan; reporting upward defeats that.
Distractors treat visibility to a manager or length as the purpose.

items.prompt: A team's retrospectives keep surfacing the same three problems every sprint, and nothing changes. Which is the most likely root cause?

options.label: The team lacks a facilitator from outside, since members cannot honestly criticise processes they take part in daily.
Improvement ideas are discussed but never turned into specific, owned actions placed in the next sprint's plan.
The problems are probably unfixable, so the team should stop retrospectives and track the issues in a management report.
The retrospective is held too often, so the team lacks enough new problems to discuss and repeats the same ones.

rubric: Recurring issues usually mean no concrete, owned follow-up reaches the sprint backlog.
Distractors blame frequency, facilitation or fatalism rather than the missing action loop.

items.prompt: A team splits every story by layer: one for the database, one for the API, one for the UI. Stories are often carried over, and demos at the review show nothing usable. What is the core problem?

options.label: Layer-based slices deliver no usable value until all of them integrate, so work looks progressed but is not done until late.
The team has too many developers, so work is spread across layers instead of everyone swarming on one single large story.
The Product Owner writes too many stories, and reducing the number would let the team focus on completing each one fully.
The stories are too small, so the overhead of planning each one consumes most of the capacity the team has for the sprint.

rubric: Horizontal slicing postpones integration and value; vertical slices give a usable increment.
Distractors misattribute the problem to story size, team size or backlog volume.

items.prompt: Which observations indicate a team is using Scrum in name only, with practices that undermine its empirical basis? Select all that apply.

options.label: The team estimates backlog items in story points.
The retrospective is skipped whenever a deadline is close.
The Product Owner changes the sprint scope mid-sprint without talking to the developers.
The team sets a Sprint Goal at planning.
The review is a demo shown only to the team, with no stakeholders giving feedback.

rubric: Uncontrolled scope changes, no stakeholder feedback and skipped retrospectives remove inspection and adaptation.
Story points and Sprint Goals are normal Scrum practice.

items.prompt: A team marks stories 'done' at the sprint review, but a separate tester then finds many defects in the following sprint, and fixes interrupt new work. Velocity looks steady at 28 points. What best explains the situation?

options.label: Velocity is steady, so the process is healthy, and the interruptions are just normal noise that every team has to absorb.
The Definition of Done excludes testing, so 'done' items are not releasable and the real remaining work is hidden in later sprints.
The testers are too strict, so defects that real users would never meet are being reported and eating the developers' time.
The sprint is too long, so shortening it to one week would stop defects from appearing in the work that has been completed.

rubric: Without testing in the Definition of Done, velocity overstates delivered value and defects become hidden carry-over.
Distractors blame testers, trust the metric, or treat sprint length as the cause.

items.prompt: A support team gets unpredictable urgent requests daily, each needing a few hours, and cannot predict next week's work. Criteria: smooth flow, quick response, limited work in progress. Which approach fits best?

options.label: Neither, because only teams with predictable work can use a visual board or any limit on work in progress effectively.
Scrum with a sprint backlog frozen for the sprint, because a fixed scope will teach requesters to plan their needs earlier.
Kanban with WIP limits and a pull system, because continuous flow suits unpredictable arrivals better than a fixed sprint commitment.
Scrum with four-week sprints, because longer sprints absorb urgent requests while the team keeps a stable commitment.

rubric: Kanban's continuous flow and WIP limits suit unpredictable, short, interrupt-driven work.
Distractors force fixed commitments onto volatile demand or reject boards.

items.prompt: Mid-sprint, a senior stakeholder asks for an urgent feature. Criteria: protect the Sprint Goal, keep the team's commitment credible, stay transparent. Which response is best?

options.label: The developers refuse any change, because scope is locked at planning and every request must wait for the next review.
The Product Owner adds it quietly and asks the team to absorb it through overtime, keeping the original scope visible.
The Product Owner checks whether it threatens the Sprint Goal, and if not, agrees with the team to swap it for similar-sized work.
The Scrum Master adds it to the sprint backlog at once, since senior stakeholders' priorities always override the team's plan.

rubric: Scope may be renegotiated if the Sprint Goal is safe, with trade-offs made visible by swapping items.
Distractors either ignore the Goal, rigidly refuse, or hide extra load.

items.prompt: Requirements change weekly, stakeholders can give feedback every week, and a team of five wants to limit ceremony overhead. Criteria: fast feedback, low wasted work. Which sprint length is best justified?

options.label: No fixed length, since ceremonies are optional once requirements change often and the team can review whenever ready.
Six weeks, since a long sprint gives stakeholders a bigger increment to review at one time and lets the team plan less.
Four weeks, since fewer ceremonies leave more time to build, and requirements will settle once the sprint has started.
One week, since feedback arrives weekly and a short cycle limits work built on outdated requirements.

rubric: Sprint length should match the rate of change and feedback availability; short cycles reduce waste.
Distractors prioritise less ceremony over feedback or drop the timebox.

items.prompt: Judge which risk most threatens Scrum's empirical process, whose basis is transparency so the team can inspect and adapt honestly.

options.label: The Product Owner reorders the backlog between sprints after speaking to a customer about new priorities, without first consulting the whole team.
The team's velocity differs by a few points from one sprint to the next because of holidays, unplanned sickness and a new joiner ramping up.
A retrospective ends early because the team ran out of topics after discussing a few improvement ideas and agreeing on one experiment.
Under deadline pressure the team quietly weakens its Definition of Done, so 'done' no longer means the same each sprint.

rubric: A quietly eroded Definition of Done destroys transparency and hides debt, so inspection is misleading.
Other options are normal variation or healthy behaviour.

items.prompt: Management proposes ranking teams by velocity and rewarding the highest. Criteria: valid measurement, healthy behaviour, real value delivered. What is the best critique?

options.label: Points are team-relative, so cross-team comparison is invalid and rewarding it invites inflated estimates.
Velocity is comparable across teams only if each team re-estimates its backlog monthly, so the proposal needs a re-estimation rule first.
The flaw is mainly timing: velocity is reported only at sprint end, so daily reporting would make team rankings fair and reliable.
The idea is sound if points are converted to hours by a standard formula, which makes teams comparable and removes gaming.

rubric: Velocity is a local planning aid; using it as a target invites gaming and is not comparable.
Distractors propose other flawed measures or only fix reporting timing.

items.prompt: A department head proposes that every sprint backlog get two hours of written pre-approval from them before the sprint starts. Which criticisms are valid, judged against self-management and fast feedback? Select all that apply.

options.label: It shifts accountability for the Sprint Goal away from the team and the Product Owner.
It delays the start of the sprint, so feedback arrives later.
It weakens the developers' ownership of how they plan and deliver the work.
It is valuable because it removes the need for any review with stakeholders.
It guarantees better quality, since a manager inspects every task in detail.

rubric: External approval gates reduce self-management, add delay and blur accountability.
Approval does not guarantee quality or replace the review's stakeholder feedback.

items.prompt: The Product Owner wants a fixed-scope release in six sprints. The backlog holds 200 points, and the team's velocity has averaged 25 points for eight sprints. Criteria: honesty about evidence, value delivered, stakeholder trust. Which response is best?

options.label: Promise all 200 points, then ask the team to work overtime and lower the Definition of Done if they fall behind.
Re-estimate the backlog at smaller point values so that 200 points become 150, and keep the original fixed scope and date.
Delay the release date indefinitely, since Scrum teams cannot forecast and should only report progress after each sprint ends.
Show that about 150 points fit in six sprints, then agree with the Product Owner which highest-value items to deliver and which to cut.

rubric: Evidence (6 x 25 = 150) shows scope must flex; prioritising by value preserves trust and quality.
Distractors hide the gap through overtime, estimate manipulation or refusing to forecast.

items.prompt: A director wants to rank five Scrum teams by velocity and reward the highest. Judged on whether velocity is a valid cross-team performance measure, which critique is strongest?

options.label: Story points are team-relative estimates, so ranking teams is invalid and rewards inflating estimates over delivering value
Velocity is comparable once adjusted for team size, so the ranking only needs a per-person normalisation factor applied
Velocity ignores how many stories are finished, so ranking by story counts would be objective and comparable across teams
Velocity is valid across teams only when sprint lengths match, so the ranking is sound once all run two-week sprints

rubric: Points are calibrated by each team, so they are not a shared unit and rewarding them invites inflation (Goodhart effect).
Distractors treat velocity as a normalisable physical quantity.

items.prompt: About 35% of a team's capacity goes to unpredictable production incidents, and sprints keep missing their goals. The team wants to keep Scrum's cadence and meaningful goals. Which adjustment best fits?

options.label: Let incidents enter the sprint as they arrive, because the team commits to the backlog and adapts at the review
Extend sprints to six weeks so incident work averages out and the goal can still cover the full planned capacity
Reserve capacity matching the measured incident rate and set the Sprint Goal on the remaining capacity only
Drop Sprint Goals and commit only to an item list, since interrupts make any goal impossible to protect

rubric: Using the observed interrupt rate for planning keeps cadence and a protectable goal.
Longer sprints and dropping goals remove feedback or focus without addressing the interrupts.

items.prompt: A team's Definition of Done excludes performance and security testing, which a separate hardening sprint handles before each release. Judged against the need for a potentially releasable increment every sprint, what is the strongest critique?

options.label: Specialist testing belongs outside the DoD because developers lack the expertise and including it would reduce velocity
The DoD is acceptable because the Product Owner approved each story, and approval is what defines completion in Scrum
Hardening sprints are fine but should be cut to one week so the release cadence stays aligned with sprint reviews
Undone work accumulates as hidden debt, so increments are not releasable and release cost and risk become unpredictable

rubric: A DoD that omits required quality work leaves the increment not releasable and hides remaining work.
Distractors accept deferral by shortening it, excusing it, or equating PO approval with Done.

items.prompt: Retrospectives for three sprints listed the same problem, unclear acceptance criteria, and each ended with 'communicate better'. Judged by likelihood of real change, which retrospective output is best?

options.label: A list of five improvements across refinement, communication and tooling so each suspected root cause is addressed in the next sprint
A team rule that stories need written criteria approved by the Product Owner before they can enter a sprint backlog, enforced by the Scrum Master
Escalation to management so the Product Owner is asked to supply more detailed criteria in future stories, with progress reviewed monthly
One experiment: the PO and a developer co-write criteria before refinement ends, checked next sprint against rework

rubric: A single small, owned, measurable experiment is the most likely to change behaviour.
Distractors are heavy rules, diffuse lists, or external mandates that bypass team ownership.

items.prompt: Midway through a sprint, a competitor launch makes the Sprint Goal pointless for the business. The team has finished 3 of 8 items. Judged by Scrum accountabilities and value, what is the best response?

options.label: The team quietly swaps in new goal work, since the backlog is living and no formal step is needed
Developers finish the sprint unchanged, since changing scope mid-sprint breaks the commitment and cancelling is not allowed
The Scrum Master cancels the sprint, since protecting the team from wasted effort is their accountability
The Product Owner cancels the sprint, done items are reviewed, and the rest are re-estimated and reordered at new planning

rubric: Only the Product Owner can cancel a sprint, and doing so stops wasted work while keeping transparency.
Distractors misassign authority or deny that cancellation is possible.

items.prompt: A vendor contract proposes paying per story point delivered. Which are sound criticisms of this scheme? Select all that apply.

options.label: Points are relative to the team, so the vendor controls the payment unit and can inflate it over time
Points measure output, not outcomes, so payment could reward features that nobody uses
Payment tied to points rewards skipping unpointed quality work such as testing and refactoring
Points cannot be added across sprints, so any per-sprint payment total would be meaningless
Points convert exactly to hours, so the contract would simply be equivalent to hourly billing

rubric: The unit is self-set, output-focused and encourages cutting unpointed work.
Points can be summed and do not convert exactly to hours.

items.prompt: In a team's Daily Scrum, each developer reports yesterday's work to the attending manager while the others tune out. Sprint goals are met, but impediments surface late. Judged against the Daily Scrum's purpose, which change is best?

options.label: Extend it to 30 minutes so impediments get detailed discussion and the manager can direct the action on each one
Developers plan the next 24 hours around the Sprint Goal, talking to each other, with the manager absent
Move to written updates in the tracker so the manager reads them each morning and meeting time goes to development
Keep the three-question format but rotate who facilitates so every developer takes a turn running the status report

rubric: The event belongs to developers for inspecting progress toward the goal and replanning.
Distractors keep the status-report-to-manager pattern.

items.prompt: Next sprint's candidates come from three stakeholders: an invoice export, a login fix, two onboarding tweaks and a report filter. Which Sprint Goal best gives the sprint coherence while keeping flexibility?

options.label: Improve the product in general, leaving the team free to choose which items to finish as the sprint unfolds
Let new customers send a first invoice in one session; the login fix and report filter may be dropped
Deliver all five items so each of the three stakeholders sees progress on their request this sprint
Complete 30 story points from the top of the backlog to give a measurable target without forcing a theme

rubric: A goal tied to one outcome with negotiable extras gives focus and room to adapt.
Distractors are a delivery list, a capacity number or a vague aim.

items.prompt: A 40-point 'new checkout' item cannot fit in a two-week sprint. Which splitting design delivers value and feedback every sprint?

options.label: Split by role: design tasks first, build tasks second, test tasks third, so each phase has clear ownership
A thin vertical slice: guest checkout with one payment method end to end, then add methods, discounts and saved cards
Split by layer: database sprint, then API sprint, then UI sprint, so each person works in their specialty
Keep it whole across two sprints and count velocity only once finished, so the estimate stays honest

rubric: Vertical slices produce a working increment that can be inspected each sprint.
Layer, role or whole-item splits delay feedback and releasable value.

items.prompt: A team spans UTC-8, UTC+1 and UTC+8; only one hour overlaps between two zones and none among all three. Which working agreement set best preserves inspect-and-adapt?

options.label: Written async Daily Scrum, live planning and review times rotated across zones, retrospective input gathered beforehand
Hold all events at the Product Owner's convenient hour, since one fixed time keeps the events consistent for everyone
Split into three zone-based sub-teams with separate backlogs and sprints, merging their work at a monthly integration
Drop the Daily Scrum and Review, rely on tracker updates, and keep planning to the single overlapping hour only

rubric: Async daily sync with rotated live events shares the burden and keeps feedback loops.
Distractors fix one zone's convenience, drop events, or fragment the team.

items.prompt: Design a team-health measure set that must not compare individuals, must give early warning, and must reflect customer outcomes. Which set meets all three?

options.label: Velocity per sprint, percentage of sprint scope completed and burndown slope, reported to management for each team every sprint
Individual story points completed, hours logged per task and bugs per developer, shown on a shared team dashboard
Number of releases, lines of code merged and tickets closed, summarised monthly to show productivity trends over time
Cycle time distribution, escaped defects per release and customer satisfaction trend, reviewed in team retrospectives

rubric: Flow, quality and customer measures are team-level and lead outcomes.
Distractors are individual, output-only or management-reporting measures.

items.prompt: A team splits time between features and support requests. Constraints: stakeholders need a regular review cadence, urgent defects need a response within a day, and work in progress must stay bounded. Which design fits all?

options.label: Two-week sprints where support requests wait for next planning and only features appear on the board
Pure Kanban with no timeboxes, reviewing on request, and every support item treated as top priority on arrival
A Scrum team for features and a Kanban team for support, reviewed separately, with no shared WIP limit
Two-week sprints with a WIP-limited board, a capped expedite lane for urgent defects, and a review at each end

rubric: Only this design provides cadence, a fast lane and bounded WIP together.
Others miss cadence, the one-day response, or a WIP bound.

items.prompt: Three teams build one product and must deliver one integrated increment each sprint. Which design elements are needed? Select all that apply.

options.label: One Product Backlog ordered by a single Product Owner
An integrated increment from all teams inspected every sprint
A project manager assigning tasks to each team's developers to ensure alignment
A shared Definition of Done that every team meets at minimum
Separate backlogs and goals per team, integrated at the end of the quarter

rubric: One backlog, a common DoD and frequent integration create a single increment.
Separate backlogs with late integration and task assignment break self-management and integration.

items.prompt: A medical-device team must provide audit evidence and regulator sign-offs yet wants iterative delivery. Which design best keeps both?

options.label: Skip evidence during sprints and reconstruct it from the tracker and commits when an audit is announced
Exempt regulated items from sprints and run them in a waterfall track with its own sign-off gates, beside the Scrum team's other work
Put traceability and review evidence in the Definition of Done, involve the quality reviewer in refinement, and release on cadence
Run sprints for development, then a separate documentation phase where evidence is compiled and signed off before each regulated release

rubric: Building compliance into Done and involving reviewers keeps increments releasable and auditable.
Distractors defer or separate compliance, recreating late-phase risk.
